title: Name 3 Criterion Films Recommended To You That (DID NOT) Butter Your Muffin

commenti.body:
400 Blows - my first watch I think I expected something more, like a bigger film. After watching it I felt cheated. It took me years to try to watch it again. Now I can appreciate the film, but the first time it felt like it didn’t meet the expectations I had set.

8 1/2 - I love Fellini.  La Strada is one of my favourite movies. A movie about a guy making movies made by a guy whose movies I loved? I thought it would be a no brainer. But this movie should be the dictionary definition of self indulgent. This is just my opinion from only watching it once. Maybe I should revisit it.

Brazil - there’s some really cool stuff In here at the set design is unforgettable and De Niros performance was really unique, but I didn’t find the movie had as much to say as I had been made to believe. Its attempt to be kafkaesque comes off more in the work than in the art. I’ve come to realize other than Monty Python and 1 or 2 films, Terry Gilliam just isn’t my bag

Did not care for The Friends of Eddie Coyle. Some parts were OK, like the heist, and Robert Mitchum did a fantastic job. But damn, talk about going nowhere. Left very emotionally unfulfilled, and there’s a lot of emotions inherent in the plot beats that could’ve been present (guilt, fear, anger, love) but weren’t.

Mickey and Nicky felt like watching an amateur theatre company doing improv for 90 minutes. The characters were insufferable, the direction was unfocused, the camerawork and lighting was dull and uninspired. 

I went in wanting to like it but couldn't wait for it to be over.

Haha are you me? I feel the same way about all three of these movies. 8 1/2 feels like such a wank to me, but I also am predisposed to find self-serious films about filmmakers/filmmaking pretty annoying for some reason.

And I’ll likely get some hate for this, but Night of the Hunter has got to be my single most disappointing film watching experience likely ever. The kids are terrible, Mitchum is so hammy as to feel like he’s acting in a sketch show, and the whole story is so simple and childish, I honestly had to double check the DVD case to make sure I was watching the right film. Just honestly can’t understand how the film is so well regarded.
Yeah, 8 1/2 did nothing for me

Not sure if it's in the Collection, but it's on the Criterion Channel - Synecdoche, NY. I generally enjoy Kaufman: I like formal conceits and messing with the fourth wall. For me this one just went too far into solipsism. The conceit in itself is that he just keeps spiraling further and further into his bleak self (or self-image) without really getting anywhere, and just as a personal matter I have very little patience for that - including when people, myself or others, do the real-world version of this in the psyche. I don't think it's poorly made or an unworthy experience to explore, it's just resoundingly not for me. (By contrast, I am *fascinated* by DAU, which is the closest anyone has ever come to doing what's portrayed in the movie for real, but there are a lot of other factors involved that make it more interesting to me. Not least that Khrzhanovsky actually, you know, did it, and it's also not literally, openly about feeling sorry for himself. It's vaguely evil, rather than annoying.)

I think I'd have an even bigger problem with it if I watched it again now, since I actually have problems with my autonomic nervous system and what he's doing is exactly what I refused to do when it happened. It would take me back to a really bad place. But at the time I saw it it was nothing so personal, I just felt like I wanted him to get on with it - whatever "it" might be. Something, anything.

L’Atalante just didn’t engage me at all. I don’t mind old films, I don’t mind slow films, but this was a chore. It didn’t “click”.

Breathless also didn’t click for me. And I went in wanting to love it, but I felt distanced from it. Like I was watching it in a film class or a museum rather than a theater.

I love Night of the Hunter but I can’t disagree with any of those thoughts. The scene of Mitchum cutting his way through the bush with his tiny knife is so crazy looking. I remember making fun of that scene and a couple “film Bros” started grilling me and I just had to laugh.

I will say I have come around on 400 Blows I can now appreciate how good it is, but that first viewing had me angry
Yeah, out of the films you listed, The 400 Blows is quite a good film I think, but the first time I watched it, I definitely had the reaction of “Oh, is that it?” when it finished.
I also found L'Atalante a bit disappointing. Not a bad film but I wasn't particularly moved or engaged by it and it just sort of happened.
What made me love 400 Blows was watching the rest of the films in the series, so I could see the boy grow up. That was terrific, and makes 400 Blows part of a larger whole.

L’Aventura bored me to tears and felt like it had no payoff. I found nothing redeeming about it.

Solaris was just far inferior to 2001 in every way. 

Rashaman was fine but not great. I thought the point it was trying to make was actually very simple and not that interesting.

My top 3 for this category would probably be 8 1/2, 12 Angry Men and Au hasard Balthazar.

8 1/2: quite a shallow film without much real meaning, very self indulgent, aimless and self-referential, and I didn't find it particularly entertaining or engrossing. Found it a real slog towards the end.  
12 Angry Men: this is the main classic I have never understood the love for. It really isn't very complex or well thought out, and the one dimensional characters and their experiences are borderline unbelievable in how unrealistic they are. It is also a very simplified and idealized view of the justice system. Au hasard Balthazar: I didn't care for the horse or main characters at all, the performances are emotionless, the empathy element I felt was the main purpose of the film since there's no plot. Also found it very boring and uninteresting.

Honorable mentions: Stalker, The Exterminating Angel
[removed]

I know I’m in the minority - but I thought ‘The White Ribbon’ - and indeed most of Haneke’s ouvre - was indolent shit.

The same could be said of Lars Von Trier only with more pejoratives and swears.

Misery-guts horseshit like that is just so utterly uninteresting to me. The whole movement’s bereft.

Why would I spend whatever amount of money or invest probably three fucking hours of my life to indulge the aspects of myself that I instinctually run from daily?

‘Oh but don’t you see? Mankind’s true nature is miserable.’

Fuck up - I know that already - that’s why I watch films. Because it’s a method of expression that lets you think a little bit higher - a little bit outside of yourself.

It’s so incomprehensible to me how these guys with an earnest talent for composing films choose to spend their time actively slinging shit in the shit pile rather than - y’know - telling a story that might just elevate their fellow man.

Self-indulgent, indolent shit.

**Stalker:** 

I actually fell asleep a couple of times despite watching it with my friend. There are some stunning shots in that film, but the story didn't do it for me.

**Boyhood:**

Granted it's been 10 years since I saw it and my film tastes have changed since then but... Apart from being a "groundbreaking experiment", it's just a very regular film isn't it?


**Raging Bull:**

Just not my cup of tea.
How did you find La Dolce Vita? I tend to think of these two films as a pair.
I liked it not my favourite of his but it was relatively enjoyable. It’s a little long and yes has some of the same problems I have with 8 1/2, my favourite FF film is either La Strada or Amarcord

I agree Night of the Hunter is the Emperor's New Clothes of film. Not scary at all. Intentionally campy at best, unintentionally funny at worst. I saw this on its first public screening in NYC in 1980s after having been banned for 20 years ...the audience was roaring with laughing at how campy /bad it was. Reports on Megalopolis remind me of this.

I tried to trash Night of the Hunter in the s/Film sub and the auto moderator wouldn't accept my post. I swear I don't know how that film continues to get positive press. Most shambolic film to be critically acclaimed.
Same here, but instead of Stalker I would say Misery. Oh god, what a waste of brain cells for me 🫠

After Hours was Scorsese getting his mojo back. He was pretty out of it when Paramount at the time backed out of Last Temptation of Christ, so After Hours was him just doing a small-scale lark to reignite his enthusiasm for filmmaking again. It was always going to be meager compared to Taxi Driver.
Ah, that’s insightful.

8 1/2 is definitely self indulgent but imo that's the point and theme of the film. Usually films like these explore subtle things about life and that film was about the inner confusion and turmoil. It was spiritual to me. I liked it

I swear there is a film podcast where as one segment of the show one of the hosts talks about a "poor" Criterion film; but my memory is very blurry on that. I know that it was a podcast of which I only listened to a single episode, so I can't even remember the name. But maybe someone else knows what I am talking about.

>As a lover of sci-fi and Andrei Tarkovsky's Mirror (1975) I was underwhelmed. I understood its themes of humanity's profound mysteries being internal, rather than external, but man did I struggling to get through this. It's definitely beautiful but its cryptic plot and monotone dialogue almost put me to sleep.

No, apparently you appreciated very little of what Tarkovsky offered in Solaris.  Its plot is not cryptic but simple.  Further, and perhaps strangely, Tarkovsky is on record that he dislikes science fiction, and that he does not make science fiction movies (re: Stalker, Solaris):

>QUESTION. Apparently, you have always been interested in the problems of scientific and technological revolution? You are one of the few directors who make science fiction films... A. >TAPKOVSKY. You are wrong. First, many people work in this genre. Secondly, you judge me as a director of science fiction films, apparently, by Solaris. If you've watched Stalker carefully, you wouldn't say that--I hope you don't get the impression that it's a sci-fi movie. In any case, we have done everything in our power to exterminate the signs of this genre in the picture. If we talk about Solaris, I think that the main drawback of this work lies precisely in the fact that the presence of genre features and peculiarities is too noticeable in it. I have to say that I am not a fan of science fiction at all. Rather the opposite... (Andrei Tarkovsky answers questions from students of Moscow State Technical University 1981)

And:

>I was no more interested, therefore, in the fantastic plot of Stalker than I had been in the story-line of Solaris. Unfortunately the science fiction element in Solaris was nonetheless too prominent and became a distraction. The rockets and space stations--required by Lem's novel--were interesting to construct; but it seems to me now that the idea of the film would have stood out more vividly and boldly had we managed to dispense with these things altogether (Sculpting in Time p.199).
